text: Chapter 8, the URL shortener. Let's see how it works in a few minutes.

We create one hundred million short URLs a day, and we must keep going for ten years. That is three hundred sixty-five billion records. A short code can use zero to nine, lowercase letters, and uppercase letters. That is sixty-two characters. Six characters give only about fifty-seven billion combinations. Not enough. Seven characters give three and a half trillion. That fits.

Approach one: hash the long URL. The book computes an MD5 hash, written in hexadecimal, and keeps the first seven characters as the short code. But each hex digit has only sixteen values. Seven digits give about two hundred sixty-eight million codes, far below three hundred sixty-five billion. In practice you would keep more hash bits and convert them to Base62.

The trouble is that different long URLs can produce the same short code. That is a collision. The fix: append a predefined string to the long URL, hash again, and check the database, until you find a free code. The book also adds a Bloom filter. If it says definitely not present, use the code. If it says possibly present, you still check the database.

Approach two: first get a globally unique ID, then convert it to Base62. In the book's example, a thirteen-digit ID is divided by sixty-two again and again. Each remainder maps to one character. Read the characters from the last remainder to the first, and you get the short code.

So which one do you pick? Hashing needs no ID generator, but collisions can happen and must be handled. Base62 never collides, as long as the IDs are unique. But it needs an ID generator, and sequential IDs make neighboring short codes easy to guess.

Here is the creation flow. First, look up the long URL in the database. If it already has a short code, return it. If not, ask the ID generator for a unique ID, convert it to Base62, and save the ID, the short code, and the long URL together in the database.

Redirecting is a different path. A user clicks the short link, and we check the cache first. On a miss, we query the database and put the result back in the cache. Then we return a redirect response, and the browser visits the long URL. Reads outnumber writes about ten to one, so this is where we optimize.

There are two kinds of redirect. A three-oh-one is permanent. The browser may cache it and go straight to the long URL next time, skipping our service. That saves traffic, but we can't count the clicks. A three-oh-two is temporary. Every click passes through our service, which suits analytics. In practice, cache headers matter too.

Remember three things. When creating, guarantee uniqueness: Base62 is an encoding, and hashing can collide. When redirecting, check the cache first. And three-oh-one versus three-oh-two depends on whether you need click statistics.
